statement: A complex linear space with an inner product is called a complex Euclidean space; the term unitary space is also used. One example is the complex vector space V_n(C).
quotes: A complex linear space with an inner product is called a complex Euclidean space. (Sometimes the term unitary space is also used.)

statement: In a complex linear space an inner product (x, y) is a complex number satisfying the same axioms as a real inner product, except that symmetry is replaced by (x, y) = conjugate of (y, x). The scalar multiplier in the homogeneity axiom may be any complex number, and the companion relation (x, cy) = conjugate(c) (x, y) follows.
quotes: In a complex linear space, an inner product $(x, y)$ is a complex number satisfying the same axioms as those for a real inner product, except that the symmetry axiom is replaced by the relation
In the homogeneity axiom, the scalar multiplier c can be any complex number.

statement: The four properties an inner product is required to satisfy for all x, y, z and all real scalars c: (1) (x,y) = (y,x) (commutativity, or symmetry); (2) (x, y+z) = (x,y) + (x,z) (distributivity, or linearity); (3) c(x,y) = (cx,y); and (x,x) > 0 if x is not the zero element. Apostol states these properties and regards them as axioms.
quotes: That is, we state a number of properties we wish inner products to satisfy and we regard these properties as axioms.

statement: A real linear space with an inner product is called a real Euclidean space. These are the examples Apostol is primarily interested in, and proofs given for V_n carry over verbatim to any real Euclidean space.
quotes: A real linear space with an inner product is called a real Euclidean space.
Therefore, the very same proof is valid in any real Euclidean space.

statement: The dot product x . y of two vectors in V_n, defined in Chapter 12 by the sum of the products of corresponding components. It is the concrete product in terms of which lengths and angles in V_n were defined, and it is the model that the inner product generalizes; in V_n one may take (x, y) = x . y.
quotes: In our study of $V_{n}$ , we defined lengths and angles in terms of the dot product.

statement: A subset S of a Euclidean space V is called an orthogonal set if (x, y) = 0 for every pair of distinct elements x and y in S. Example: the trigonometric system in C(0, 2pi) with the integral inner product is an orthogonal set.
quotes: A subset S of V is called an orthogonal set if $(x, y) = 0$ for every pair of distinct elements x and y in S.
so S is an orthogonal set. Since no member of S is the zero element, S is independent.

These properties do not depend on the choice of inner product.

statement: THEOREM 15.12: if {e_1, ..., e_n} is an orthonormal basis for a finite-dimensional Euclidean space V of dimension n, then for every pair x, y in V the inner product equals the sum of (x, e_i) times the conjugate of (y, e_i) (Parseval's formula). Taking x = y gives ||x||^2 as the sum of |(x, e_i)|^2.

statement: THEOREM 15.11: if V is a finite-dimensional Euclidean space of dimension n and S = {e_1, ..., e_n} is an orthogonal basis, then the components of x relative to the ordered basis are c_j = (x, e_j)/(e_j, e_j). statement: A real linear space V is said to have an inner product if to each pair of elements x, y there corresponds a unique real number (x, y) satisfying four axioms: symmetry, distributivity (linearity), homogeneity in the scalar, and positivity for nonzero x. Apostol defines the product axiomatically rather than by a specific formula.

statement: In a real Euclidean space V the angle between two nonzero elements x and y is the number theta in [0, pi] with cos theta = (x, y) / (||x|| ||y||). The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality shows the quotient lies in [-1, 1], so exactly one such theta exists.
quotes: DEFINITION. In a real Euclidean space V, the angle between two nonzero elements x and y is defined to be that number $\theta$ in the interval $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ which satisfies the equation
\cos \theta = \frac {(x , y)}{\| x \| \| y \|}.\tag{15.6}

statement: Part (d) of Theorem 15.9: ||x + y|| <= ||x|| + ||y|| for all elements x and y of a Euclidean space. The equality sign holds if x = O, if y = O, or if y = cx for some c > 0. The proof expands ||x + y||^2 and applies the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
quotes: (d) $\|x + y\| \leq \|x\| + \|y\|$ (triangle inequality).
The equality sign holds in (d) if $x = O$ , if $y = O$ , or if $y = cx$ for some $c > 0$ .

statement: A linear space equipped with an inner product. When the term Euclidean space is used without further designation the space may be real or complex, and the theorems of the chapter hold in either case. The inner product is what introduces the metric concept of length into such a space.
quotes: When we use the term Euclidean space without further designation, it is to be understood that the space can be real or complex.
The inner product can be used to introduce the metric concept of length in any Euclidean space.

statement: In a Euclidean space V, two elements x and y are called orthogonal if their inner product is zero. The zero element is orthogonal to every element of V, and it is the only element orthogonal to itself.
quotes: DEFINITION. In a Euclidean space V, two elements x and y are called orthogonal if their inner product is zero.
The zero element is orthogonal to every element of V; it is the only element orthogonal to itself.

statement: THEOREM 15.10: in a Euclidean space V, every orthogonal set of nonzero elements is independent. In particular, in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with dim V = n, every orthogonal set consisting of n nonzero elements is a basis for V.
quotes: THEOREM 15.10. In a Euclidean space V, every orthogonal set of nonzero elements is independent.
In particular, in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space with dim V = n, every orthogonal set consisting of n nonzero elements is a basis for V.

statement: On C(a, b), the linear space of all real-valued functions continuous on [a, b], an inner product of f and g is defined by the integral of f(t)g(t) over [a, b]. The function values f(t) and g(t) play the role of the components, and integration takes the place of summation.

statement: An orthogonal set is called orthonormal if each of its elements has norm 1. Dividing each element of an orthogonal set by its norm produces an orthonormal set.
quotes: An orthogonal set is called orthonormal if each of its elements has norm 1.
Dividing each $u_{n}$ by its norm, we obtain an orthonormal set $\{\varphi_0,\varphi_1,\varphi_2,\ldots \}$ where $\varphi_{n} = u_{n} / \| u_{n}\|$ .
